source_claims.statement: HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems.
HTTP is foundational to World Wide Web data communication.
HTTP uses request-response in the client-server model.
Browsers, crawlers, voice browsers, mobile apps and other software can act as user agents.
HTTP supports intermediate caches and proxies; some headers are hop-by-hop and others end-to-end.
Web resources are located through URL/URI schemes http and https.
HTTP/0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3 are the versions listed with their introduction years/statuses.
HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource; HTTP/1.1 introduced reusable persistent connections.
HTTP/2 adds binary header representation, multiplexed streams, and server push.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP.
HTTP data exchange uses reliable transport; TCP is the pre-HTTP/3 standard choice.
HTTP/1.1 messages have start line, header fields, blank line, and optional body.
HTTP methods classify requested actions and have safety, idempotence, and cacheability properties.
GET is intended to retrieve without modifying server state, while other methods can modify state.
Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY in the supplied source.
Idempotent methods include PUT, DELETE and safe methods; POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily idempotent.
GET, HEAD and POST are defined as cacheable in the source table.
HTTP response status codes are three-digit classes 1xx through 5xx.
HTTP is stateless; application sessions can be implemented with cookies, hidden variables or other mechanisms.
HTTP provides Basic and Digest authentication through challenge-response.
HTTPS is the popular encrypted form of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 message headers use ASCII lines terminated by CRLF.
HTTP/1.1 supports conditional retrieval, chunked transfer and byte-range serving.
Tim Berners-Lee and CERN are credited with HTTP's invention/development.
HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.
SPDY influenced HTTP/2 and was developed by Google.
HTTP/2 was published in 2015 and HTTP/3 was standardized in 2022.
RFC 9110/9111/9112/9113/9114 are the current semantic/caching/version documents listed by the source.

value.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
value.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

value.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
value.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

value.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
value.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

value.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
value.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

value.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
value.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

value.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
value.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

value.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
value.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

value.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
value.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

value.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
value.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

value.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
value.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

value.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
value.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

value.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
value.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

value.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

value.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
value.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

value.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
value.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

value.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
value.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

value.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
value.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

value.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
value.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

value.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
value.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

value.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
value.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

value.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
value.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

value.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
value.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

value.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
value.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

value.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
value.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

value.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
value.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

value.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

value.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
value.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

value.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
value.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.

misconceptions.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
misconceptions.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

misconceptions.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

misconceptions.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
misconceptions.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

misconceptions.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
misconceptions.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

misconceptions.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
misconceptions.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

misconceptions.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

misconceptions.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
misconceptions.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

misconceptions.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
misconceptions.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

misconceptions.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

misconceptions.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
misconceptions.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

misconceptions.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
misconceptions.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

misconceptions.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
misconceptions.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
misconceptions.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

misconceptions.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
misconceptions.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
misconceptions.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
misconceptions.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

misconceptions.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
misconceptions.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

misconceptions.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
misconceptions.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

misconceptions.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
misconceptions.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.
